newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RALLYING-WORLD RALLY CHAMPIONSHIP BATTLE SET TO HOT UP.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-WORLD RALLY CHAMPIONSHIP BATTLE SET TO HOT UP.

text.p: The battle for this year's World Rally Championship is set to hot up this weekend at the New Zealand Rally at Manukau in Auckland.

Reigning world champion Tommi Makinen, of Finland, currently leads the title chase in his Mitsubishi, but will have to perform well to fight off his main rival, Briton Colin McRae, winner of this event four times in the last five years.

"I think this rally will be really good for us and it's actually a nice event to drive," said Makinen. "In the last two years I have been unlucky in that I've gone off the road when leading, so hopefully this year, with the car even faster than before, I can be the winner."

McRae, though, is equally confident. "I have great memories of New Zealand obviously," said the newly-wed. "We're reaching a crucial point in the championship now and, despite Tommi only being 10 points ahead of us, nothing short of victory is going to be enough to stop him running away with the championship.
"Having said that, he's never finished higher than sixth in New Zealand, and I'm confident I can pull it off."

Makinen's team-mate Briton Richard Burns won the event last season and is also a potential contender, as is McRae's Subaru partner Kenneth Eriksson, of Sweden, who narrowly missed out on victory last season.

"Of course I would like to win again, but the opposition is going to be even tougher this weekend," said Burns. "On paper this is going to be the closest rally of the season yet -- and that's saying something.
"I believe all six factory-backed drivers are in with a serious shout for the outright victory. I'm really looking forward to it."

But it is the Ford team that start the event as dark-horses for victory. The pairing of Spaniard Carlos Sainz and Finn Juha Kankkunen finished first and second on the Acropolis Rally in June and modifications made to their cars in recent weeks are certainly going to improve their chances in New Zealand.
"I've completed quite a few miles in private testing and won a rally in Finland with the new gearbox and it's a big step forward," explained Sainz, who lies third in the title chase.

Kankkunen added: "The team can't do any better than it did in Greece. First and second is unbeatable. If we maintain that sort of form, and if we enjoy the luck that you need in this sport to be successful, then there's no reason why we can't produce another good result."
The New Zealand Rally takes place in the dense forests and farmland of the North Island and is a big test of driver skill and car performance.

The first leg on Sunday comprises of nine stages to the north of Auckland, while leg two, the longest and most demanding of the event, takes the teams south of the city for a further eight stages. The final leg will see the drivers tackle six more stages before finishing back in Auckland on Tuesday afternoon.
